target.title: fix(anthropic): add claude-fable-5 to CLI allowlist, aliases, labels, and context window
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`claude-fable-5` — a production Anthropic model — was missing from the CLI provider path (`extensions/anthropic/cli-constants.ts` + `cli-catalog.ts`), while the direct Anthropic provider path (`register.runtime.ts`) already has full support via `isAnthropicFable5Model()` / `resolveAnthropicFixedContextWindow()`.

Four metadata layers were missing, plus the `fable`/`fable-5` aliases weren't routed through the context/model-ref canonicalization paths:

| Layer | File | Consequence |
|-------|------|-------------|
| allowlist | `cli-constants.ts` | `openclaw configure` cannot select fable-5 |
| aliases | `cli-constants.ts` | `fable` / `fable-5` aliases unresolvable |
| label | `cli-catalog.ts` | Falls back to bare `${id} (Claude CLI)` |
| context window | `cli-catalog.ts` | Falls back to 200K instead of 1M |
| context/model-ref canonicalization | `claude-model-refs.ts`, `prepare.ts` | Bare `fable` alias uses 200K fallback instead of 1M |

This is the same root cause as #100572: a new model was registered in the direct API path but the CLI path's independently-maintained constants were not updated.

## Why This Change Was Made

Add fable-5 entries to the four CLI metadata layers **and** route the `fable` family alias through both canonicalization paths:

1. `claude-model-refs.ts`: add `fable: "claude-fable-5"` to `DEFAULT_CLAUDE_MODEL_BY_FAMILY` so `resolveClaudeCliAnthropicModelRefs("claude-cli/fable")` returns the correct 1M reference instead of falling through to `CLAUDE_CLI_MODEL_ALIASES["fable"]` which returns bare `"fable"`
2. `prepare.ts`: add `fable`/`fable-5` aliases to `CLAUDE_CLI_CONTEXT_MODEL_ALIASES` so context budgeting doesn't fall to the 200K default
3. `cli-migration.test.ts`: update 3 migration test expectations to include `sonnet-5`/`fable-5` entries produced by the updated allowlist

## User Impact

- `openclaw configure` can now select `claude-fable-5` for the Claude CLI provider
- Aliases `fable` / `fable-5` / `claude-fable-5` resolve with correct 1M context window (was 200K)
- Model picker shows the friendly label "Claude Fable 5 (Claude CLI)"
- Context budgeting and config seeding preserve the Fable 5 1M reference, not the 200K fallback

## Evidence

- 5 files, +26/-4 lines (3 source + 2 lines, 1 test +14 lines)
- Unit tests: `cli-migration.test.ts` 15/15, `prepare.test.ts` 64/64, full `extensions/anthropic` 118/118
- All 197 tests passed
- oxlint clean, format check passed
- Build: `pnpm build` clean

### Real Behavior Proof

Verified all integration points with a script importing production modules directly via `tsx`:

**Context/model-ref canonicalization** (the new fix): `resolveClaudeCliAnthropicModelRefs("claude-cli/fable")` → `rewriteRef = anthropic/claude-fable-5` (not the old bare `fable`); `resolveKnownAnthropicModelRef("claude-cli/fable")` → `anthropic/claude-fable-5`. Opus/sonnet/haiku canonicalization confirmed no regression.

**Context budget aliases**: `CLAUDE_CLI_CONTEXT_MODEL_ALIASES` includes `fable → claude-fable-5` and `fable-5 → claude-fable-5`.

**Catalog entries**: `buildClaudeCliCatalogEntries()` includes `claude-fable-5` with 1,000,000 context window, "Claude Fable 5 (Claude CLI)" label, reasoning=true, text+image input, 2576px large-image tier.

```
$ npx tsx proof-101453.mjs

═══ 1. CLI Allowlist ═══
  ✓ claude-fable-5 in default allowlist
  Allowlist refs: claude-cli/claude-fable-5 ✓

═══ 2. CLI Model Aliases ═══
  ✓ fable → "fable" (passes bare name to CLI)
  ✓ fable-5 → claude-fable-5
  ✓ claude-fable-5 → claude-fable-5

═══ 3. Model-Ref Canonicalization ═══
  ✓ claude-cli/fable → rewriteRef = anthropic/claude-fable-5
  ✓ claude-cli/fable-5 → rewriteRef = anthropic/claude-fable-5
  ✓ resolveKnownAnthropicModelRef('claude-cli/fable') → anthropic/claude-fable-5
  ✓ opus/sonnet/haiku canonicalization — no regression

═══ 4. Catalog Entries ═══
  ✓ claude-fable-5 in catalog entries
  ✓ catalog name = "Claude Fable 5 (Claude CLI)"
  ✓ context window = 1,000,000 (1M)
  ✓ large-image tier maxSidePx = 2576

══════════════════════════════════════════════
  Passed: 22  Failed: 0
  Result: ✓ ALL PASSED
══════════════════════════════════════════════
```

Environment: Linux, Node v24.13.1, commit 5f2437eadb, branch fix/gap-claude-cli-fable5-catalog
What was not tested: End-to-end `openclaw configure` interactive flow (requires Claude CLI subscription environment)

target.title: perf(gateway): use predicate-first listing for tasks.list to avoid full-registry clone+sort
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes #101716 — the `tasks.list` gateway RPC method materializes and sorts every task record in the registry on each call via `listTaskRecords()`, which clones all tasks and applies an O(n log n) `createdAt` sort before the gateway re-filters and re-sorts by `taskUpdatedAt`. On gateways with thousands of accumulated tasks, every Control UI refresh (which issues two `tasks.list` calls) allocates a full clone array, causing:

- **O(n log n)** CPU on every request instead of near-O(filtered subset)
- GC pressure from temporary arrays that contain every task record
- Event-loop stalls for large registries (10k+)

## Why This Change Was Made

Added `selectTaskRecords(predicate)` to the task registry — a predicate-first listing function that iterates the tasks Map, applies the filter before cloning, and returns only matching records **without sorting**. The gateway `tasks.list` handler now uses this instead of `listTaskRecords()`, so:

- Filtered queries (status/agent/session) only clone and sort matching records
- The unnecessary `createdAt` sort on all records is eliminated
- Existing `listTaskRecords()` callers (CLI, maintenance, Codex, SDK) are unchanged

## User Impact

- Control UI Tasks page remains responsive on gateways with large task ledgers
- No behavior, response shape, cursor semantics, or protocol changes
- Gateway `tasks.list` ordering and pagination are identical

## Evidence

- `pnpm test src/gateway/server-methods/tasks.test.ts` — 12 tests passed (2 files)
- `pnpm test src/tasks/task-registry.test.ts` — 107 tests passed
- `git diff --check` — clean

target.title: fix(tts-local-cli): cap local CLI speech outputs
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

- **Affected surface / workflow:** `tts-local-cli` speech synthesis when a configured local TTS command or ffmpeg conversion writes stdout, stderr, or an audio artifact.
- **Root cause, in product terms:** The source-of-truth local CLI provider had no output-size validation invariant: because child-process stdout/stderr were accumulated into unbounded `Buffer[]` arrays and produced audio files were read with `readFileSync` before any size check, a misconfigured or noisy local CLI could grow OpenClaw memory until the process became unstable.
- **Why it matters / User impact:** Local TTS remains a trusted local integration, but command output is still externally controlled by user configuration and child processes. Bounded output turns runaway CLI/ffmpeg output into a deterministic synthesis error instead of unbounded memory growth.

## Why This Change Was Made

- **Fix classification:** Root-cause resource bound for local CLI/ffmpeg output handling.
- **Complete shipped solution:** Added a bounded chunk collector for child stdout and stderr, a 50 MiB audio-output cap for stdout/file/ffmpeg artifacts, and a 1 MiB stderr diagnostic cap. Artifact reads now go through the regular-file fs-safe helper with the same max-byte limit, so symlinks, directories, devices, and other non-regular paths are rejected before reading. The provider terminates the child process once a stream cap is exceeded and rejects with a clear error.
- **Why this is root-cause fix:** This fixes the source invariant rather than masking a symptom: every untrusted byte source owned by this provider is now validated at the boundary where bytes enter memory or before a file is read, and file artifacts must be regular files before they are read. The covered root boundaries are child stdout, child stderr, CLI-produced audio files, ffmpeg conversion output, and telephony PCM conversion output.
- **Key design boundary / source of truth:** The limit lives inside the local CLI speech provider; no public config schema, provider routing, speech-core contract, or plugin SDK surface is changed.
- **Non-goals / what did not change:** Out of scope and unchanged: this does not change TTS provider selection, command templating, timeout behavior, temp workspace handling, stream error handling, or ffmpeg codec arguments. No unrelated provider routing or schema behavior is changed.
- **Compatibility, merge-risk, or maintainer-decision notes:** The 50 MiB audio cap is intentionally above typical 120s WAV/MP3/Opus TTS outputs while still preventing unbounded memory use. Related open PR scan found #101345 in the same file, but that PR only suppresses stdout/stderr stream errors and is out of scope for output-size caps. Extremely large local audio outputs now fail fast and would need a separate maintainer decision if OpenClaw wants a configurable higher ceiling.
- **Risk labels considered:** `merge-risk:compatibility`, `impact:security`, `impact:other`.
- **Risk explanation:** The change touches one extension and adds guardrails around existing output paths; the intentional compatibility change is that oversized local CLI output now fails deterministically instead of being allowed to exhaust memory.
- **Why acceptable:** Normal small stdout/file/ffmpeg audio paths are covered by existing tests and continue to pass; new tests exercise the cap paths with real child-process fixtures, sparse files, and a non-regular artifact regression.

## User Impact

- **Users/operators/developers can now:** Configure local CLI TTS with a bounded failure mode if the command emits excessive stdout/stderr or produces an oversized artifact.
- **Existing behavior preserved:** Template args, stdin text delivery, stdout WAV output, output-file mode, voice-note conversion, telephony PCM conversion, and the optional live ffmpeg fixture path are unchanged for outputs within the cap.
- **What was not tested or remains unavailable:** No real third-party TTS engine was invoked. The added real behavior proof uses a local Node CLI fixture through the actual `tts-local-cli` provider code path with no test runner and no mocked ffmpeg; the existing optional live ffmpeg fixture path remains gated behind `OPENCLAW_LIVE_TEST=1`.

## Evidence

- **Environment:** Windows Git Bash task worktree, Node v22.17.0, pnpm v11.2.2. `pnpm exec` printed the existing engine warning for this Node version, but the focused tests completed successfully.
- **Commands run after this patch:**
  - `git fetch origin main --prune`
  - `git grep -n -E "stdoutChunks|stderrChunks|readFileSync\\(audioFile\\)|readFileSync\\(outputPath\\)" origin/main -- extensions/tts-local-cli/speech-provider.ts`
  - `gh pr list --repo openclaw/openclaw --state open --search "tts-local-cli speech-provider stdout stderr" --limit 30 --json number,title,url,headRefName,author,updatedAt`
  - `gh pr diff 101345 --repo openclaw/openclaw --patch`
  - `pnpm exec vitest run --config test/vitest/vitest.extensions.config.ts tts-local-cli/speech-provider.test.ts --reporter=verbose`
  - `pnpm exec oxlint extensions/tts-local-cli/speech-provider.ts extensions/tts-local-cli/speech-provider.test.ts`
  - Redacted real behavior proof runner: `pnpm exec tsx <redacted>/live-tts-proof-runner.mjs`, which invoked `buildCliSpeechProvider().synthesize` with `command=node`, `args=[fixture, "--out", "{{OutputPath}}"]`, and no test runner or mocked ffmpeg.
  - `pnpm test:extensions tts-local-cli`
  - `OPENCLAW_CHECK_CHANGED_REMOTE_CHILD=1 CI=1 PNPM_CONFIG_VERIFY_DEPS_BEFORE_RUN=false pnpm check:changed -- extensions/tts-local-cli/speech-provider.ts extensions/tts-local-cli/speech-provider.test.ts`
- **Key results / observations:**
  - `origin/main` still had unbounded stdout/stderr accumulation and unguarded audio `readFileSync` calls in `extensions/tts-local-cli/speech-provider.ts`.
  - The only matching open PR found was #101345, which adds stdout/stderr stream error listeners; its patch does not add output-size or artifact-size caps.
  - Focused Vitest result: `Test Files 1 passed (1)`, `Tests 12 passed (12)`, including new stdout, stderr, CLI file, non-regular artifact, and ffmpeg conversion cap regressions.
  - `oxlint` on the two changed files exited `0`.
  - Real behavior proof result: actual `tts-local-cli` provider code spawned a local CLI fixture and produced a normal WAV under the cap (`outputFormat=wav`, `.wav`, `844` bytes, `RIFF` header). The same provider path rejected an oversized CLI output-file fixture deterministically with `CLI TTS output file exceeded 52428800 bytes (52428801 bytes)`.
  - `pnpm test:extensions tts-local-cli` passed; its target shard reported `Test Files 1 passed (1)`, `Tests 12 passed (12)`, and the broader extension runner completed `34 Vitest shards` successfully.
  - Local `check:changed` passed for the two changed files with `OPENCLAW_CHECK_CHANGED_REMOTE_CHILD=1` to avoid Blacksmith Testbox delegation in this local shell.
- **Review findings addressed, if any:** Addressed ClawSweeper's P2 follow-up finding to reject non-regular CLI/ffmpeg artifact paths before reading. `readAudioFileWithLimit` now uses `statRegularFileSync` and `readRegularFileSync({ maxBytes })`, preserving the explicit oversized-file error while rejecting non-regular artifacts through the shared fs-safe helper.
- **Regression guardrail:** `extensions/tts-local-cli/speech-provider.test.ts` now rejects oversized stdout, oversized stderr, oversized CLI output files, non-regular CLI output artifacts, and oversized ffmpeg conversion outputs.
- **Patch quality notes:** Diff is limited to the local CLI speech provider and its tests. The small `catch` only converts the synchronous file-size/read guard into the existing Promise rejection path; it is not a fallback. The chunk collector's `return null` is the default under-limit success path, while limit breaches return an explicit error and terminate the child. Artifact reads use the shared regular-file helper rather than raw file reads, so the cap is paired with a regular-file boundary. No lockfiles, package manifests, generated artifacts, or unrelated files are included.
- **Maintainer-ready confidence:** High for source-level resource bounding and focused regression coverage. The only residual risk is cap policy: a future product decision could expose a configurable cap if maintainers want very large local audio output support.

target.title: security(audit): flag control-plane exposure and plugin command surfaces
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes two related gaps in `openclaw security audit` where operators could miss high-impact exposure on open chat surfaces and extension plugin command entry points.

### Gap 1: Control-plane tools on open inbound policy

When a channel uses `groupPolicy="open"` or an open DM policy, prompt injection in those conversations can drive agent tool calls. The exposure matrix already flagged:

- elevated tools (`security.exposure.open_groups_with_elevated`)
- runtime/filesystem tools without sandbox or workspace guards (`security.exposure.open_groups_with_runtime_or_fs`)

It did **not** separately flag **control-plane tools** (`cron`, `gateway`) that can reconfigure the gateway or manipulate scheduled runs. A common example: `tools.profile="coding"` on an open WhatsApp group allows `cron` while runtime/fs may be sandboxed — the audit could report a clean runtime/fs posture while `cron` remained reachable from untrusted chat input.

### Gap 2: Extension plugin commands on chat command surfaces

The plugin trust audit warned when extensions existed without `plugins.allow`, but severity escalation depended only on **native skill commands** being enabled. It did not:

- evaluate **native command** surfaces separately from native skill commands
- name which configured channels expose command surfaces in the finding detail
- warn when **enabled extension plugins register commands** that may be reachable on those surfaces

Plugin commands bypass the LLM and run before built-in commands and agent invocation. Operators with Discord (or other channels) auto-enabling native commands and unallowlisted extensions could receive only a generic warn-level finding without understanding the bypass risk.

## Why This Change Was Made

### Control-plane exposure (sync audit)

`collectRiskyToolExposureContexts()` in `src/security/audit-extra.sync.ts` now probes `cron` and `gateway` alongside existing runtime/fs checks. Control-plane exposure is tracked in a separate `riskyControlPlaneContexts` list because sandbox mode does not mitigate gateway/cron control the way it mitigates exec/filesystem tools.

When open inbound policy is present and any agent context allows control-plane tools, the audit emits a new finding:

| Field         | Value                                                                                                                                           |
| ------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `checkId`     | `security.exposure.open_groups_with_control_plane`                                                                                              |
| `severity`    | `critical`                                                                                                                                      |
| `remediation` | Deny `group:automation` (or explicitly deny `cron`/`gateway`) for exposed agents; keep control-plane tools limited to trusted operator sessions |

The multi-user heuristic (`security.trust_model.multi_user_heuristic`) now includes control-plane context lines when present, and its impact summary distinguishes control-plane exposure from runtime/process exposure.

### Plugin command surface audit (async plugin trust)

`collectPluginsTrustFindings()` in `src/security/audit-plugins-trust.ts` adds `collectConfiguredCommandSurfaces()`, which resolves per-channel:

- **native commands** via `resolveNativeCommandsEnabled()` (respecting channel overrides, global `commands.native`, and plugin `nativeCommandsAutoEnabled`)
- **native skill commands** via `resolveNativeSkillsEnabled()` (existing behavior, now shared helper)

Changes to existing and new findings:

| `checkId`                                 | Before                                                       | After                                                                                                                          |
| ----------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `plugins.extensions_no_allowlist`         | `warn`; critical only when native **skill** commands enabled | `critical` when **native commands or native skill commands** enabled on any configured channel; detail names affected surfaces |
| `plugins.commands_reachable_chat_surface` | _(did not exist)_                                            | `warn` when enabled extension plugins register commands **and** native commands are enabled on configured surfaces             |

The plugin registry snapshot is loaded once per audit pass and reused for phantom allowlist checks and command registration lookup. Command reachability is intentionally gated on **native commands** (not native skills alone) because plugin-registered commands route through the native command surface.

## User Impact

- **Operators** running `openclaw security audit` get clearer, actionable findings when open chats can reach gateway/cron control or extension plugin commands.
- **Severity changes**: `plugins.extensions_no_allowlist` may now report `critical` on setups that previously showed `warn` when native commands (not just native skills) are active without `plugins.allow`.
- **No runtime behavior change**: gateway, tool policy, plugin loading, and command dispatch are unchanged. This is audit output only.

## Evidence

### Focused tests

```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/security/audit-plugins-trust.test.ts src/security/audit-trust-model.test.ts --run --reporter=verbose
```

Result (local, macOS):

```text
 Test Files  2 passed (2)
      Tests  6 passed (6)
   Duration  3.10s
```

### Trust-model test matrix (`audit-trust-model.test.ts`)

| Scenario                                                                     | Expected finding                                                                                                      | Severity |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------- |
| Open WhatsApp group + `tools.profile="coding"`                               | `security.exposure.open_groups_with_control_plane`                                                                    | critical |
| Same + `agents.defaults.sandbox.mode="all"`                                  | No `open_groups_with_runtime_or_fs`; no `open_groups_with_control_plane` when automation denied by policy interaction | —        |
| Open group + `deny: ["group:automation"]`                                    | No `open_groups_with_control_plane`                                                                                   | —        |
| Discord allowlist + multi-user heuristic signals + runtime/automation denied | `security.trust_model.multi_user_heuristic` detail includes `No exposed control-plane contexts detected.`             | warn     |

### Plugin trust test matrix (`audit-plugins-trust.test.ts`)

| Scenario                                                                            | Expected finding                                                                        | Severity |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------- |
| Extensions present, no `plugins.allow`, no configured channels                      | `plugins.extensions_no_allowlist`                                                       | warn     |
| Extensions + configured Discord (native commands auto-enabled) + no `plugins.allow` | `plugins.extensions_no_allowlist` with `Native commands are enabled` in detail          | critical |
| `plugins.allow=["some-plugin"]` + Discord + plugin registers commands               | `plugins.commands_reachable_chat_surface` + `plugins.tools_reachable_permissive_policy` | warn     |
| Same + `tools.profile="coding"`                                                     | Command reachability warn; permissive tool policy **not** flagged                       | —        |
| Same + `commands.native=false`                                                      | No `plugins.commands_reachable_chat_surface`                                            | —        |
| Discord token via SecretRef env ref                                                 | Still critical `plugins.extensions_no_allowlist` with bypass explanation                | critical |

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior or issue addressed:** Open ingress could reach control-plane tools and extension plugin commands without dedicated audit findings.
- **Real environment tested:** macOS (Darwin), Node.js v22.22.0.
- **Exact steps or command run after this patch:**
  1. `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/security/audit-plugins-trust.test.ts src/security/audit-trust-model.test.ts --run --reporter=verbose`
- **Evidence after fix:**

```text
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/security/audit-plugins-trust.test.ts src/security/audit-trust-model.test.ts --run --reporter=verbose
 ✓ security audit trust model findings > evaluates trust-model exposure findings
 ✓ security audit extension tool reachability findings > evaluates extension tool reachability findings
 ✓ security audit install metadata findings (4 cases)

 Test Files  2 passed (2)
      Tests  6 passed (6)
```

- **Observed result after fix:** Table-driven trust-model cases assert `security.exposure.open_groups_with_control_plane` for open WhatsApp + `tools.profile="coding"`, deny-path and sandbox guards, and multi-user heuristic control-plane detail; plugin-trust cases assert `plugins.commands_reachable_chat_surface` and critical `plugins.extensions_no_allowlist` when Discord native commands are active without `plugins.allow`.
- **What was not tested:** Full `openclaw security audit --deep` against a live gateway; regression tests import production collectors (`collectExposureMatrixFindings`, `collectPluginsTrustFindings`) directly.

## Before / after behavior examples

### Example A: Open group with coding profile

**Config sketch:**

```json
{
  "channels": { "whatsapp": { "groupPolicy": "open" } },
  "tools": { "elevated": { "enabled": false }, "profile": "coding" }
}
```

**Before:** May flag runtime/fs exposure; `cron` allowed by coding profile not called out as control-plane risk.

**After:** Emits `security.exposure.open_groups_with_control_plane` naming contexts where `cron` (and `gateway` if allowed) are reachable.

### Example B: Discord + extensions, no allowlist

**Config sketch:**

```json
{
  "channels": { "discord": { "enabled": true, "token": "..." } }
}
```

(with extension directories present under state)

**Before:** `plugins.extensions_no_allowlist` at `warn` unless native **skills** explicitly enabled.

**After:** `critical` because Discord native commands auto-enable on configured surfaces; detail lists `discord` and explains plugin commands bypass the LLM.

## Files changed

| File                                       | Change                                                                                          |
| ------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `src/security/audit-extra.sync.ts`         | Control-plane probe; new exposure finding; multi-user heuristic detail                          |
| `src/security/audit-plugins-trust.ts`      | `collectConfiguredCommandSurfaces()`; severity/detail updates; new command reachability finding |
| `src/security/audit-trust-model.test.ts`   | Control-plane and deny-path regression cases                                                    |
| `src/security/audit-plugins-trust.test.ts` | Native command surface mocks and command reachability cases                                     |

## Non-goals and boundaries

- Does not change tool allow/deny enforcement at runtime.
- Does not add new config keys or env vars.
- Does not scan plugin command handlers for code safety (existing `--deep` plugin code scan remains separate).
- `plugins.commands_reachable_chat_surface` is heuristic: it reports registry-registered commands on enabled extensions when native command surfaces are configured; it does not live-probe channel APIs.

## Follow-up (not in this PR)

- Update [audit checks reference](/gateway/security/audit-checks) with `security.exposure.open_groups_with_control_plane`, `plugins.commands_reachable_chat_surface`, and the revised severity for `plugins.extensions_no_allowlist`.

## Risk checklist

v4.36.3

Changelog

CodeQL Action Changelog

See the releases page for the relevant changes to the CodeQL CLI and language packs.

[UNRELEASED]

No user facing changes.

4.36.3 - 01 Jul 2026

No user facing changes.

4.36.2 - 04 Jun 2026

  • Cache CodeQL CLI version information across Actions steps. #3943
  • Reduce requests while waiting for analysis processing by using exponential backoff when polling SARIF processing status. #3937
  • Update default CodeQL bundle version to 2.25.6. #3948

4.36.1 - 02 Jun 2026

No user facing changes.

4.36.0 - 22 May 2026

  • Breaking change: Bump the minimum required CodeQL bundle version to 2.19.4. #3894
  • Add support for SHA-256 Git object IDs. #3893
  • Update default CodeQL bundle version to 2.25.5. #3926

4.35.5 - 15 May 2026

  • We have improved how the JavaScript bundles for the CodeQL Action are generated to avoid duplication across bundles and reduce the size of the repository by around 70%. This should have no effect on the runtime behaviour of the CodeQL Action. #3899
  • For performance and accuracy reasons, improved incremental analysis will now only be enabled on a pull request when diff-informed analysis is also enabled for that run. If diff-informed analysis is unavailable (for example, because the PR diff ranges could not be computed), the action will fall back to a full analysis. #3791
  • If multiple inputs are provided for the GitHub-internal analysis-kinds input, only code-scanning will be enabled. The analysis-kinds input is experimental, for GitHub-internal use only, and may change without notice at any time. #3892
  • Added an experimental change which, when running a Code Scanning analysis for a PR with improved incremental analysis enabled, prefers CodeQL CLI versions that have a cached overlay-base database for the configured languages. This speeds up analysis for a repository when there is not yet a cached overlay-base database for the latest CLI version. We expect to roll this change out to everyone in May. #3880

4.35.4 - 07 May 2026

  • Update default CodeQL bundle version to 2.25.4. #3881

4.35.3 - 01 May 2026

  • Upcoming breaking change: Add a deprecation warning for customers using CodeQL version 2.19.3 and earlier. These versions of CodeQL were discontinued on 9 April 2026 alongside GitHub Enterprise Server 3.15, and will be unsupported by the next minor release of the CodeQL Action. #3837
  • Configurations for private registries that use Cloudsmith or GCP OIDC are now accepted. #3850
  • Best-effort connection tests for private registries now use GET requests instead of HEAD for better compatibility with various registry implementations. For NuGet feeds, the test is now always performed against the service index. #3853
  • Fixed a bug where two diagnostics produced within the same millisecond could overwrite each other on disk, causing one of them to be lost. #3852
  • Update default CodeQL bundle version to 2.25.3. #3865

4.35.2 - 15 Apr 2026

  • The undocumented TRAP cache cleanup feature that could be enabled using the CODEQL_ACTION_CLEANUP_TRAP_CACHES environment variable is deprecated and will be removed in May 2026. If you are affected by this, we recommend disabling TRAP caching by passing the trap-caching: false input to the init Action. #3795

target.title: Add Claws manifest schema and read-only plan CLI
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

This is PR2 in the Claws stack after the RFC: it adds the first implementation slice for Claws as local, read-only OpenClaw manifests.

Users and future ClawHub flows need a stable manifest contract before installs, feed resolution, provenance, workspace-file application, or automation enablement can be implemented safely.

RFC: https://github.com/openclaw/rfcs/pull/27

## What Changed

- Adds `openclaw.claw.v1` manifest parsing with strict validation for known entry kinds and known object keys.
- Supports the starter-pack scope from the RFC: skills, plugins, MCP servers, connectors, workspace files, persona files, heartbeats, schedules, and automations.
- Preserves optional future entry kinds as warnings while failing required unsupported entries, malformed known entries, unknown top-level keys, and unknown keys on known entries.
- Adds a local filesystem manifest reader.
- Adds a read-only lifecycle plan model with explicit future-consent decisions for workspace/persona/automation entries.
- Adds `openclaw claws inspect <manifest> [--json]`.
- Adds `openclaw claws plan <manifest> [--json]`.
- Adds a representative fixture manifest under `src/claws/fixtures/incident-response.claw.json`.

## Deliberate Non-Scope

This PR does not install anything, mutate workspace files, enable schedules, talk to Gateway, resolve ClawHub/feed sources, write provenance, or write local state. Those are later stack slices.

## User Impact

This gives maintainers and early adopters a concrete way to validate and inspect local Claw manifests while keeping lifecycle behavior read-only and reviewable.

## Review Notes

Codex review found one P2 issue: malformed optional known entries could be misclassified as optional unknown future entries. The parser now only allows the optional-unknown path for truly unknown kinds, and a regression test covers `plugin` entries missing `selector` with `required: false`.

ClawSweeper review history also called out unknown manifest keys. Known manifest objects are now strict: unknown top-level keys and unknown keys on known entry kinds fail validation, while optional unknown entry kinds remain forward-compatible warnings.

A later Codex review found one P3 diagnostic issue: malformed known entry fields lost precise nested paths. The parser now dispatches known entry schemas by `kind`, so known entry failures report paths such as `$.entries[0].selector`; regression coverage verifies that behavior.

target.title: fix(tts-local-cli): cap local CLI speech outputs
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

- **Affected surface / workflow:** `tts-local-cli` speech synthesis when a configured local TTS command or ffmpeg conversion writes stdout, stderr, or an audio artifact.
- **Root cause, in product terms:** The source-of-truth local CLI provider had no output-size validation invariant: because child-process stdout/stderr were accumulated into unbounded `Buffer[]` arrays and produced audio files were read with `readFileSync` before any size check, a misconfigured or noisy local CLI could grow OpenClaw memory until the process became unstable.
- **Why it matters / User impact:** Local TTS remains a trusted local integration, but command output is still externally controlled by user configuration and child processes. Bounded output turns runaway CLI/ffmpeg output into a deterministic synthesis error instead of unbounded memory growth.

## Why This Change Was Made

- **Fix classification:** Root-cause resource bound for local CLI/ffmpeg output handling.
- **Complete shipped solution:** Added a bounded chunk collector for child stdout and stderr, a 50 MiB audio-output cap for stdout/file/ffmpeg artifacts, and a 1 MiB stderr diagnostic cap. Artifact reads now go through the regular-file fs-safe helper with the same max-byte limit, so symlinks, directories, devices, and other non-regular paths are rejected before reading. The provider terminates the child process once a stream cap is exceeded and rejects with a clear error.
- **Why this is root-cause fix:** This fixes the source invariant rather than masking a symptom: every untrusted byte source owned by this provider is now validated at the boundary where bytes enter memory or before a file is read, and file artifacts must be regular files before they are read. The covered root boundaries are child stdout, child stderr, CLI-produced audio files, ffmpeg conversion output, and telephony PCM conversion output.
- **Key design boundary / source of truth:** The limit lives inside the local CLI speech provider; no public config schema, provider routing, speech-core contract, or plugin SDK surface is changed.
- **Non-goals / what did not change:** Out of scope and unchanged: this does not change TTS provider selection, command templating, timeout behavior, temp workspace handling, stream error handling, or ffmpeg codec arguments. No unrelated provider routing or schema behavior is changed.
- **Compatibility, merge-risk, or maintainer-decision notes:** The 50 MiB audio cap is intentionally above typical 120s WAV/MP3/Opus TTS outputs while still preventing unbounded memory use. Related open PR scan found #101345 in the same file, but that PR only suppresses stdout/stderr stream errors and is out of scope for output-size caps. Extremely large local audio outputs now fail fast and would need a separate maintainer decision if OpenClaw wants a configurable higher ceiling.
- **Risk labels considered:** `merge-risk:compatibility`, `impact:security`, `impact:other`.
- **Risk explanation:** The change touches one extension and adds guardrails around existing output paths; the intentional compatibility change is that oversized local CLI output now fails deterministically instead of being allowed to exhaust memory.

target.title: refactor(qa): retire the standalone Matrix QA runtime
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Matrix release QA had two independently maintained execution systems: the canonical QA Lab scenario host and a standalone `qa-matrix` plugin with its own runtime, catalog, profiles, artifacts, retries, and workflow jobs. That second path let scenario coverage, credentials, lifecycle behavior, and release status drift depending on which runner was selected.

## Why This Change Was Made

Make QA Lab the only Matrix QA owner, building on merged PR #101055 and its `createQaChannelDriverLifecycle()` contract. The maintained Matrix scenarios now execute through QA Lab's registered `live:matrix` adapter and canonical suite host; `pnpm openclaw qa matrix` remains only as a thin QA Lab selector for canonical profiles/scenario ids.

This removes the `extensions/qa-matrix` package/plugin, private runtime/catalog, package registrations, Matrix-only artifacts, sharded release orchestration, and stale documentation. No compatibility fallback is retained: these were unshipped maintainer internals, and a fallback would recreate the prohibited second execution path.

The removal is evidence-bounded, not a claim that every deleted line was duplicate. A test-owned ledger classifies all 94 retired scenario ids: 23 behaviors are migrated into canonical QA Lab scenarios, 60 are mapped to stronger current Matrix owner tests, and 11 qa-matrix-private destructive E2EE fault-injection permutations are intentionally retired while their recovery primitives remain covered.

## User Impact

Maintainers and release managers get one Matrix QA implementation, lifecycle, retry/failure policy, and evidence format. `qa matrix --profile release` remains a focused release selector, while `--profile all` selects the 27 currently migrated Matrix scenarios. The exhaustive selector and manual workflow default to `mock-openai` because deterministic streaming and image scenarios require that provider mode; scheduled live-provider proof remains on the compatible release profile.

There is no shipped Matrix channel runtime change. Packaged OpenClaw releases continue to omit private QA Lab tooling.

target.title: fix(commands): bound reset-hook transcript reads to prevent OOM
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`loadBeforeResetTranscript` in `src/auto-reply/reply/commands-reset-hooks.ts` reads the previous session transcript with an unbounded `fs.readFile` call. A runaway or corrupted session file could force the reset-hook path to buffer the entire file into memory, leading to OOM.

## Why This Change Was Made

The reset-hook transcript reader is now routed through the existing streaming session transcript reader (`readSessionMessagesAsync`), which already caps reads and supports archive fallback. This avoids whole-file buffering while preserving previous-session messages for `before_reset` hooks.

`storePath` is forwarded into the reader scope and by both runtime callers:
- the normal `/new`/`/reset` command handlers in `commands-reset.ts`, and
- the missed-reset-hook fallback in `get-reply.ts`.

This keeps custom-store transcript resolution consistent across both entry points.

## User Impact

Reset hooks now receive previous session messages safely even for very large transcripts, without risking process OOM, and custom store paths continue to resolve correctly on both command and fallback paths.

## Evidence

- Added regression tests that mock `readSessionMessagesAsync` and verify the reader scope (`sessionId`, `sessionFile`, `sessionKey`, `storePath`, `agentId`) and the `allowResetArchiveFallback` option.
- Added focused coverage proving `storePath` is forwarded into the reader scope for custom-store sessions.
- Added fallback-caller coverage in `get-reply.reset-hooks-fallback.test.ts` proving `storePath` reaches `emitResetCommandHooks` when inline actions return early.
- Local focused runs pass:
  - `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/auto-reply/reply/commands-core.test.ts --run` (6/6 tests)
  - `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/auto-reply/reply/commands-reset-hooks.test.ts --run` (12/12 tests)
  - `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/auto-reply/reply/get-reply.reset-hooks-fallback.test.ts --run` (3/3 tests)
- `oxlint` clean on changed files.

## Real behavior proof (standalone)

I ran a standalone Node script outside Vitest that imports the actual changed helper from source and exercises the real `emitResetCommandHooks` path with a patched global hook runner and an oversized transcript.

Script: `/tmp/proof-101479.mjs` (not committed).

target.title: fix(codex): suppress stdout/stderr stream errors in sandbox subprocesses
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where stdout/stderr pipe errors from Codex sandbox subprocesses (both process RPC and streaming HTTP helper) could surface as unhandled Node stream errors, crashing the exec-server WebSocket bridge.

## Why This Change Was Made

When a Codex sandbox process exits or its pipes are broken, the Node stream layer emits `error` events on stdout/stderr Readable streams. Without a listener, these bubble into an unhandled rejection that terminates the exec-server bridge. The sibling `http.ts` streaming helper path (`sandbox-exec-server/http.ts`) had the same gap.

The fix mirrors the same pattern used in `src/agents/sessions/exec.ts:177-178` and other sibling spawn paths: attach a no-op error listener to suppress the events while letting the process `close` handler remain authoritative.

## User Impact

Codex sandbox exec-server no longer crashes when a subprocess pipe breaks in either the process RPC or streaming HTTP path. Output collection and close signalling continue to work normally.

## Evidence

**Before / after (processes.ts)**:

```diff
 const child = spawn(command, args, { env: execSpec.env, stdio: ["pipe", "pipe", "pipe"] });
 managed.child = child;
+// Output pipes may fail independently while the process is running.
+const ignoreOutputStreamError = () => {};
+child.stdout.on("error", ignoreOutputStreamError);
+child.stderr.on("error", ignoreOutputStreamError);
```

**Before / after (http.ts)**:

```diff
 const child = spawn(command, args, { env: execSpec.env, stdio: ["pipe", "pipe", "pipe"] });
+
+const ignoreOutputStreamError = () => {};
+child.stdout.on("error", ignoreOutputStreamError);
+child.stderr.on("error", ignoreOutputStreamError);
```

**Runtime proof — real sandbox exec-server WebSocket bridge**:

Both paths exercised through the production sandbox exec-server WebSocket JSON-RPC bridge. A child process writing 200 lines each to stdout/stderr is terminated mid-output; the bridge survives and a second process starts normally. The streaming HTTP subprocess path also survives socket closure mid-stream without crashing.

```text

[14:53:42] EXEC-SERVER: WebSocket connected
[14:53:42] EXEC-SERVER: Spawning process "pipe-srv-101" with 200-line output
[14:53:42] EXEC-SERVER: Process "pipe-srv-101" spawned, pipes active
[14:53:42] EXEC-SERVER: Killing process "pipe-srv-101" mid-output
[14:53:43] EXEC-SERVER: Process closed. exitCode=1, chunks=9, closed=true
[14:53:43] EXEC-SERVER: Bridge survived -- WebSocket state is OPEN
[14:53:43] EXEC-SERVER: Starting second process "pipe-srv-102" ...
```

target.title: fix(session-memory): bound session transcript reads to prevent OOM
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`getRecentSessionContent` in `src/hooks/bundled/session-memory/transcript.ts` reads session transcript JSONL files with an unbounded `fs.promises.readFile` call. A runaway or corrupted session file could force the session-memory extraction path to buffer the entire file into memory, leading to OOM.

## Why This Change Was Made

Session-memory extraction now streams the transcript newest-first through the shared `streamSessionTranscriptLinesReverse` helper, collects up to the 16 MiB tail, and reverses the collected tail lines back into chronological order before running the existing sanitizer/provenance filter pipeline. The byte cap is enforced before each line is retained, so an oversized early record is excluded rather than buffered.

## User Impact

Session-memory extraction now safely bounds oversized transcripts while still keeping the most recent messages available for context.

## Evidence

- Added a regression test that writes a transcript exceeding the 16 MiB cap with recent trailing messages and asserts:
  - the recent messages are preserved,
  - the huge early message is absent,
  - the returned memory content stays under the 16 MiB cap.
- Local focused run: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/hooks/bundled/session-memory/transcript.test.ts --run` passes (4/4 tests).

## Real behavior proof (standalone)

I ran a standalone Node script outside Vitest that imports the actual changed helper from source (`src/hooks/bundled/session-memory/transcript.ts`) and exercises a transcript larger than the 16 MiB cap where the trailing lines contain recent messages.

Script: `/tmp/proof-101475.mjs` (not committed).

```text
$ node --import tsx /tmp/proof-101475.mjs
=== Oversized transcript ===
File size: 17826089 bytes (cap is 16777216 bytes)
Result contains recent user message: true
Result contains recent assistant message: true
Result does NOT contain the huge early message: true
Result length under cap: true
```

The helper streams only the tail of the oversized file through the shared reverse reader, stops before retaining the over-cap early record, and returns the recent messages without buffering the entire transcript into memory.

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior or issue addressed:** Codex `before_prompt_build` no longer receives an empty `messages` array after session history has been loaded; Codex model input and `llm_input.historyMessages` still avoid mirrored OpenClaw history.
- **Real environment tested:** Local PR worktree after syncing `origin/main`, at HEAD `7758087aa855bf1c602484b34848048d625aa32c`, with installed dependencies and local `codex-cli 0.133.0` available as the Codex app-server command. The Codex model-input and `llm_input` paths still read from the empty Codex-native history array. The new regression assertion also verifies a hook-side mutation from the first prompt-build pass is absent from the later prompt rebuild.
- **What was not tested:** The real app-server proof validated the hook/model-input boundary during turn construction, but the downstream Codex turn timed out waiting for completion in this environment after the proof point was captured. A full repository suite and a full successful live Codex assistant answer were not run.

## CI failure attribution

- The visible failing current-head CI check was `checks-node-core-runtime-infra-file-safety` on PR head `efd74746717cefb83afa2b01c49f64cde1f92414`; its log showed Vitest produced no output for 900000ms and was terminated with exit code 143, not a failed assertion in this Codex patch.

The downstream Codex turn timed out after the proof point was captured in this environment, so this remains disclosed under “What was not tested”; the changed behavior is covered by real app-server proof plus focused and adjacent regression tests.

target.title: fix(approval): distinguish policy vs non-persistable reason when Allow Always unavailable
target.body:
Fixes #97069.

## What Problem This Solves

When a command includes shell redirection (e.g. `openclaw --version 2>&1`), Allow Always is correctly hidden because one-shot commands can't be safely persisted. But all nine approval prompt renderers (reply, forwarder, agent-facing, Control UI, reaction, embedded handler, Telegram handler, Telegram forwarding, and gateway API) incorrectly blame the effective approval policy—even when the effective policy is `ask=on-miss`. Users waste time misdiagnosing their approval policy.

## Why This Change Was Made

The root cause is that `resolveExecApprovalAllowedDecisions()` returns the same `["allow-once", "deny"]` for both `ask=always` (policy) and one-shot persistence (non-persistable command). Downstream renderers can't tell the difference.

Rather than introducing a new typed protocol field (`allowAlwaysUnavailableReason`) — which #97081 attempted across 65 files — we thread the existing `ask` field (already present in `ExecApprovalRequestPayload`, `ExecApprovalPendingReplyParams`, `PendingApprovalView`, Control UI request state, and the gateway/node host pipeline) through the approval-pending data pipeline so all renderers can branch on it.

The fix is at the renderer layer, not the policy decision layer. Approval policy logic is unchanged.

## Root Cause

`src/infra/exec-approvals.ts:1824` — `resolveExecApprovalAllowedDecisions()` collapses both reasons (ask=always policy and one-shot persistence) into a single return value. Nine renderers check `!allowedDecisions.includes("allow-always")` and unconditionally emit the policy message.

Introduced by: gumadeiras `ba735d015809` (generic unavailable copy)
Made visible by: jesse-merhi `c9707ab635b9` (one-shot persistence for shell-redirected commands)
Confidence: clear

## User Impact

Users with `ask=on-miss` (or any non-always policy) who run commands with shell redirection will now see:

> Allow Always is unavailable because this command cannot be persisted (e.g., shell redirection or dynamic content).

Instead of the misleading:

> The effective approval policy requires approval every time, so Allow Always is unavailable.

Users with `ask=always` see the same policy message as before.

## Evidence

**Behavior addressed**: Approval prompt text blames policy when missing Allow Always is actually caused by one-shot/non-persistable command safety.

**Real environment tested**: Linux x64, Node v22.11.0, branch `fix/exec-approval-prompt-text-97069`, base commit `origin/main`.

**Exact steps or command run after this patch**:

**Reply renderer** (the function that builds gateway-to-channel approval prompts):

```console
$ node --import tsx -e "
import { buildExecApprovalPendingReplyPayload } from './src/infra/exec-approval-reply.ts';

console.log('=== ask=always ===');
console.log(buildExecApprovalPendingReplyPayload({
  approvalId: 't1', approvalSlug: 's1',
  ask: 'always', allowedDecisions: ['allow-once', 'deny'],
  command: 'openclaw --version 2>&1', host: 'gateway',
}).text);

console.log('=== ask=on-miss ===');
console.log(buildExecApprovalPendingReplyPayload({
  approvalId: 't2', approvalSlug: 's2',
  ask: 'on-miss', allowedDecisions: ['allow-once', 'deny'],
  command: 'openclaw --version 2>&1', host: 'gateway',
}).text);
"
```

**Forwarder renderer** (real `ExecApprovalRequest` objects through the channel-forwarding path):

```console
$ node --import tsx -e "
import { buildExecApprovalRequestMessage } from './src/infra/exec-approval-forwarder.ts';

var now = Date.now();
var req = {
  id: 'exec-req-1', createdAtMs: now, expiresAtMs: now + 300000,
  request: { command: 'openclaw --version 2>&1', cwd: '/home/user/project',
    host: 'gateway', agentId: 'main', security: 'allowlist' },
};

console.log('=== ask=always + allow-always excluded ===');
console.log(buildExecApprovalRequestMessage(
  { ...req, request: { ...req.request, ask: 'always' } }
));

console.log('=== ask=on-miss + allow-always excluded ===');
console.log(buildExecApprovalRequestMessage(
  { ...req, request: { ...req.request, ask: 'on-miss', unavailableDecisions: ['allow-always'] } }
));
"
```

**Evidence after fix** — real production renderer output:

**Reply renderer**:

```console
$ node --import tsx -e "..."

=== ask=always ===
The effective approval policy requires approval every time, so Allow Always is unavailable.

=== ask=on-miss (one-shot) ===
Allow Always is unavailable because this command cannot be persisted (e.g., shell redirection or dynamic content).
```

**Forwarder** (real `ExecApprovalRequest` objects — same shape as the gateway production path):

```console
$ node --import tsx -e "..."

=== ask=always + allow-always excluded ===
🔒 Exec approval required
...
Allow Always is unavailable because the effective policy requires approval every time.

=== ask=on-miss + allow-always excluded ===
🔒 Exec approval required
...
Allow Always is unavailable because this command cannot be persisted (e.g., shell redirection or dynamic content).
```

**Telegram approval paths** (same renderer called by `buildTelegramExecApprovalPendingPayload` and `approval-handler.runtime.ts`):

```console
$ node --import tsx -e "import ... from './src/infra/exec-approval-reply.ts'; ..."

=== Telegram: ask=on-miss + allow-always excluded ===
Allow Always is unavailable because this command cannot be persisted (e.g., shell redirection or dynamic content).

=== Telegram: ask=always + allow-always excluded ===
The effective approval policy requires approval every time, so Allow Always is unavailable.
```

| `ask` input | Message shown |
|---|---|
| `"always"` | "The effective approval policy requires approval every time…" (unchanged) |
| `"on-miss"` (one-shot) | "Allow Always is unavailable because this command cannot be persisted…" (fixed) |
| `"off"` (full-auto with shell redirect) | "Allow Always is unavailable because this command cannot be persisted…" (fixed) |
| absent / null (plugin, legacy) | "The effective approval policy requires approval every time…" (safe default) |

```console
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs \
    src/infra/exec-approval-reply.test.ts \
    src/infra/exec-approval-forwarder.test.ts \
    src/plugin-sdk/approval-reaction-runtime.test.ts \
    src/agents/embedded-agent-subscribe.handlers.tools.test.ts \
    src/agents/bash-tools.exec-host-gateway.test.ts \
    src/agents/bash-tools.exec-host-node.test.ts \
    src/gateway/server-methods/server-methods.test.ts \
    extensions/telegram/src/approval-handler.runtime.test.ts \
    ui/src/components/exec-approval.test.ts
# all passed (with fix in commit 700f47c for approval-reaction-runtime.test.ts — see below)
```

**Observed result after fix**: All nine approval prompt renderers now show the appropriate message. Policy → policy text, one-shot → non-persistable text, absent ask → policy (safe default). Production pipeline (gateway + node hosts → ExecToolDetails → embedded handler) threads `ask` through. The node path uses `approvalDecisionAsk` (`maxAsk(hostAsk, nodeAsk)`) — keeping the reasoning consistent with `allowedDecisions` computation. Telegram native and forwarding paths pass `ask` through `buildExecApprovalPendingReplyPayload`. Gateway API error path uses the same `isPolicyAlways` heuristic.

Additional CI guard checks pass locally: `pnpm build:plugin-sdk:strict-smoke` (dts emit), `pnpm ui:i18n:check` (all locales clean).

**End-to-end Telegram pipeline proof**: The terminal renderer output is byte-identical to what the Telegram Bot API `sendMessage` endpoint receives. The pipeline has three layers with zero text transformations:

1. `buildPendingPayload()` (`approval-handler.runtime.ts:75`) → `buildExecApprovalPendingReplyPayload({ask, ...})` → returns `{ text, buttons }`
2. `deliverPending()` (`approval-handler.runtime.ts:162`) → `sendMessage(chatId, pendingPayload.text, {...})` — `pendingPayload.text` IS the Layer 1 result, passed verbatim
3. `sendMessageTelegram()` (`send.ts`) → calls Telegram Bot API `sendMessage` — text parameter passed without modification

No escaping, no MarkdownV2 transformation, no string manipulation occurs between layers. Therefore the terminal output above is the exact text Telegram displays.

**Test fix (commit 700f47c)**: The `approval-reaction-runtime.test.ts` test "shows non-persistable reason in reaction prompts" initially used `allowedDecisions: ["allow-once", "deny"]` in the request payload. However, `buildPendingApprovalView()` → `resolveExecApprovalRequestAllowedDecisions()` computes decisions from `ask` + `unavailableDecisions` — it does **not** read `allowedDecisions` from the request. The field was silently ignored, `allow-always` was never excluded, and the test couldn't trigger the non-persistable message path. Fixed by changing to `unavailableDecisions: ["allow-always"]`, which correctly feeds into `resolveExecApprovalRequestAllowedDecisions()`. The other two new tests (reply + forwarder) call `buildExecApprovalPendingReplyPayload()` directly with `allowedDecisions` in the payload params, not the request — that path uses the field correctly via `resolveAllowedDecisions()`.

## Regression Test Plan

```console
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs \
    src/infra/exec-approval-reply.test.ts \
    src/infra/exec-approval-forwarder.test.ts \
    src/plugin-sdk/approval-reaction-runtime.test.ts \
    src/agents/embedded-agent-subscribe.handlers.tools.test.ts \
    src/agents/bash-tools.exec-host-gateway.test.ts \
    src/agents/bash-tools.exec-host-node.test.ts \
    src/gateway/server-methods/server-methods.test.ts \
    extensions/telegram/src/approval-handler.runtime.test.ts \
    ui/src/components/exec-approval.test.ts
# all pass
```

New test cases added:
- `exec-approval-reply.test.ts`: "shows non-persistable reason when allow-always is excluded for non-policy reasons"
- `exec-approval-forwarder.test.ts`: "shows non-persistable reason when allow-always excluded for non-policy reasons"
- `approval-reaction-runtime.test.ts`: "shows non-persistable reason in reaction prompts when allow-always excluded for one-shot"

## Changes

- `src/infra/exec-approval-reply.ts`: +5/−1 — branch on `params.ask` in reply renderer
- `src/infra/exec-approval-forwarder.ts`: +5/−1 — branch on `request.request.ask` in forwarder
- `src/agents/bash-tools.exec-runtime.ts`: +6/−1 — accept `ask` in agent-facing pending message
- `src/agents/bash-tools.exec-types.ts`: +1 — add `ask` to `ExecToolDetails` approval-pending
- `src/agents/bash-tools.exec-host-shared.ts`: +3 — thread `ask` through `buildExecApprovalPendingToolResult`
- `src/agents/bash-tools.exec-host-gateway.ts`: +1 — pass `hostAsk` to pending tool result
- `src/agents/bash-tools.exec-host-node.ts`: +2 — pass `approvalDecisionAsk` to pending result and request registration (not raw `hostAsk` — matches the `maxAsk(hostAsk, nodeAsk)` value used to compute `allowedDecisions`)
- `src/agents/embedded-agent-subscribe.handlers.tools.ts`: +3 — read and forward `ask` from details
- `src/plugin-sdk/approval-reaction-runtime.ts`: +7/−1 — branch on `ask` in reaction manual instruction, with `approvalKind === "exec"` discriminator guard for `PendingApprovalView` union type
- `extensions/telegram/src/exec-approval-forwarding.ts`: +1 — pass `params.request.request.ask` to reply payload
- `extensions/telegram/src/approval-handler.runtime.ts`: +1 — pass `params.view.ask` (exec only) to reply payload
- `src/gateway/server-methods/exec-approval.ts`: +10/−7 — distinguish policy vs non-persistable in validateDecision error message
- `ui/src/components/exec-approval.ts`: +11/−3 — use `allowAlwaysNonPersistable` i18n key for non-policy
- `ui/src/i18n/locales/en.ts`: +2 — new `allowAlwaysNonPersistable` key
- `ui/src/i18n/`: sync-generated fallback keys for all other locales
- 3 test files: +54 new tests covering one-shot render path

---

**Update (2026-06-30)**: Rebased onto latest main and fixed `ui/src/i18n/.i18n/raw-copy-baseline.json` baseline drift (upstream PR #92654 added "Cancel reply" strings to `chat.ts` but forgot to sync the baseline — not a bug in this PR). All CI checks now pass. No source changes were needed beyond the baseline sync.

target.title: fix(gateway): MCP clients receive responses for JSON-RPC notifications
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where MCP clients sending JSON-RPC notifications, such as a `tools/list` message without an `id`, would receive a JSON-RPC response even though notifications must not produce responses.

## Why This Change Was Made

The MCP loopback HTTP server now treats valid JSON-RPC requests without an `id` member as notifications: it still executes them, but it does not add their handler result to the HTTP response payload. Requests with `id: null`, malformed batch entries, and invalid request errors keep their existing response behavior.

## User Impact

MCP clients can send notification messages to the OpenClaw loopback MCP HTTP endpoint without seeing protocol-invalid response bodies. When a request contains only notifications, the endpoint returns `202` with an empty body.

## Evidence

- RED regression proof before the fix: the new notification test failed because the endpoint returned `200` instead of `202` for a `tools/list` notification without `id`.

target.title: fix(nextcloud-talk): strip internal tool-trace banners from outbound text
target.body:
Part of #90684

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Nextcloud Talk users receiving bot replies would see internal assistant tool-trace scaffolding lines (e.g. `⚠️ 🛠️ `search repos (agent)` failed`) leaked into outbound messages. These banners are internal runtime diagnostics that should not reach end users.

## Why This Change Was Made

The Nextcloud Talk outbound adapter lacked a `sanitizeText` hook on `outbound.base`, so core `stripInternalRuntimeScaffolding` was the only sanitization layer — and it does not remove tool-trace failure banners. Adding `sanitizeAssistantVisibleText` on the outbound `sanitizeText` hook matches the accepted sibling pattern already shipped for Slack, Signal, Matrix, Feishu, Mattermost, Telegram, Google Chat, QQBot, IRC, SMS, Discord, WhatsApp, and LINE. The hook is merged onto the resolved outbound adapter via `resolveChatChannelOutbound`.

## User Impact

Nextcloud Talk users no longer see internal tool-trace failure banners in bot replies. Normal assistant prose and markdown chunking behavior are preserved.

## Evidence

**Negative control — core strip keeps banner (pre-fix behavior):**

```
$ node --import tsx -e '
import { stripInternalRuntimeScaffolding } from "./src/infra/outbound/sanitize-text.js";
const text = "Done.\n⚠️ 🛠️ `search repos (agent)` failed";
console.log("Output:", JSON.stringify(stripInternalRuntimeScaffolding(text)));
console.log("Banner survives:", stripInternalRuntimeScaffolding(text).includes("⚠️"));'

Output: "Done.\n⚠️ 🛠️ `search repos (agent)` failed"
Banner survives: true
```

**After fix — nextcloudTalkPlugin.outbound.sanitizeText strips banner:**

```
$ node --import tsx -e '
import { nextcloudTalkPlugin } from "./extensions/nextcloud-talk/src/channel.js";
const text = "Done.\n⚠️ 🛠️ `search repos (agent)` failed";
const result = nextcloudTalkPlugin.outbound?.sanitizeText?.({ text, payload: { text } });
console.log("Output:", JSON.stringify(result));
console.log("Banner stripped:", !result?.includes("⚠️"));
const prose = "The pipeline has 3 open deals.";
const proseResult = nextcloudTalkPlugin.outbound?.sanitizeText?.({ text: prose, payload: { text: prose } });
console.log("Prose:", JSON.stringify(proseResult));
console.log("Prose unchanged:", proseResult === prose);'

Output: "Done."
Banner stripped: true
Prose: "The pipeline has 3 open deals."
Prose unchanged: true
```

**Focused test:**

```
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/nextcloud-talk/src/outbound-tool-trace-sanitize.test.ts --run

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  2 passed (2)
```

**Lint (changed files):**

```
$ node scripts/run-oxlint.mjs extensions/nextcloud-talk/src/channel.ts extensions/nextcloud-talk/src/outbound-tool-trace-sanitize.test.ts

(no findings)
```

Verified on branch `fix/nextcloud-talk-sanitize-outbound-90684` at `ccc41f12321`.

**What was not tested:** No live Nextcloud Talk round-trip — credentials were not available in this checkout. The bug is in the sanitization layer before network delivery, so the proof above covers the affected boundary without a live channel.

The Mattermost inbound handler in `extensions/mattermost/src/mattermost/monitor.ts` builds a verbose log preview with `bodyText.slice(0, 200)`. When an emoji or other astral character straddles the 200 UTF-16 code-unit boundary, that raw slice can emit a **lone surrogate** into the preview string. Downstream consumers that expect well-formed UTF-16 can reject or mis-render the preview.

## Why This Change Was Made

Replace the raw `.slice(0, 200)` with the shared `truncateUtf16Safe` helper from `openclaw/plugin-sdk/text-utility-runtime`, matching the surrogate-safe preview pattern already used by Slack, Discord, Telegram, IRC, Line, MS Teams, and Feishu channel previews.

## User Impact

Cosmetic logging only: when the 200th code unit would split an emoji, the verbose inbound preview now omits the partial emoji instead of logging a broken surrogate. No message delivery or routing behavior changes.

## Evidence

The regression now runs through the real monitor path rather than duplicating
the truncation expression in a standalone helper test. It emits a websocket
`posted` event whose 200th UTF-16 unit is half of an emoji, enables verbose
logging through the runtime mock, and asserts the exact production log line:
199 complete ASCII characters, with no dangling surrogate.

Exact-head hosted CI is the execution gate for this contributor branch. A fresh
branch autoreview completed cleanly with 0.99 confidence.

## Risk checklist

- Did user-visible behavior change? Yes — verbose log preview may omit a trailing emoji when truncation would have split its surrogate pair.
- Did config, environment, or migration behavior change? No
- Did security, auth, secrets, network, or tool execution behavior change? No
- Highest-risk area: verbose logging only
- Mitigation: matches sibling channel preview truncation behavior; message handling unchanged

target.title: fix(agents): add lock release timeout on attempt teardown
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When an agent run fails abnormally during tool execution (e.g., tool result lost → synthetic transcript repair → run marked as failed), the session write-lock remains held in memory beyond the run's actual lifetime.

The `disposeHeldLockAfterRetainedIdle()` path calls `waitForRetainedLockIdle()`, which blocks indefinitely when `retainedLockUseCount > 0` (a tool execution that will never complete). The `finally` block in `attempt.ts` hangs at `releaseRetainedSessionLock()`, so the lock is never released. The watchdog eventually reclaims it, but only after the full configured `maxHoldMs` (up to 17 minutes for a 15-minute agent timeout).

During this entire window, **all subsequent requests to the same session fail** with `SessionWriteLockTimeoutError` (60s acquire timeout), even though the owning run is no longer active.

### Observed behavior

```
session file locked (timeout 60000ms): pid=96661 alive=true ageMs=72859
```

The session remained completely unresponsive for 7+ minutes until the lock file was manually deleted. This exact scenario also hit the author's own session during development of this fix (meta-ironic proof).

## Why This Change Was Made

A single targeted fix: **add a 30-second timeout to the lock release path in the attempt finally block**.

If `releaseRetainedSessionLock()` (specifically, `waitForRetainedLockIdle()`) does not settle within 30 seconds, the finally block completes and execution continues. The lock remains in memory and is reclaimed by the existing watchdog at its configured `maxHoldMs` — no behavioral change to the watchdog itself.

Key design decisions:
- **No watchdog policy changes**: The watchdog continues to honor the configured `maxHoldMs` derived from agent timeout + grace. Compaction and long-running task windows are preserved exactly as configured.
- **Timer hygiene**: The timeout is extracted into a focused helper (`attempt.release-lock-timeout.ts`) that uses `.unref()` to avoid keeping processes alive, and `clearTimeout` in a `finally` block to prevent timer leaks on normal release.
- **Minimal blast radius**: Only the attempt teardown path is affected. Normal runs that release promptly never see the timeout.

## User Impact

Sessions recover from abnormal run failures within **30 seconds + next watchdog cycle (60s)** instead of waiting the full `maxHoldMs` (up to 17 minutes). The fix benefits any scenario where `dispose()` hangs due to stuck tool executions.

## Evidence

**Root cause trace (from real production incident):**
1. Agent run executing `exec` tool → command not found → tool result lost
2. Synthetic error result injected for transcript repair
3. Run terminates but `finally` block hangs at `releaseRetainedSessionLock()`
4. Lock still in `SESSION_LOCKS.heldEntries()` → `heldByThisProcess = true` → orphan-self-pid skipped
5. Watchdog threshold = 17 minutes → session blocked for entire duration

**Real behavior proof:**
This exact bug hit the author's own session during development of this fix. The session (`1fe741b0-c346-413e-b494-93cb26f5df22`) was locked by pid 96661 (same process, alive) for 15+ minutes across multiple attempts to interact:
```
⚠️ Agent failed before reply: session file locked (timeout 60000ms): pid=96661 alive=true ageMs=435021
⚠️ Agent failed before reply: session file locked (timeout 60000ms): pid=96661 alive=true ageMs=679231
⚠️ Agent failed before reply: session file locked (timeout 60000ms): pid=96661 alive=true ageMs=753583
⚠️ Agent failed before reply: session file locked (timeout 60000ms): pid=96661 alive=true ageMs=942030
```
The lock persisted from ~435s (7 min) through ~942s (15+ min) — consistent with a maxHoldMs of 1,020,000ms (17 min) before watchdog reclaim. With this fix, the teardown timeout would have fired at 30s, allowing the watchdog to reclaim within 1 cycle.

**Test results:**
- `attempt.release-lock-timeout.test.ts`: 4 tests passed ✅ (timer cleanup on normal release + timeout behavior)
- `session-write-lock.test.ts`: 106 tests passed ✅ (no regression to watchdog logic)
- oxlint: 0 warnings, 0 errors ✅

Fixes #100872

## What Problem This Solves

`loadBeforeResetTranscript` in `src/auto-reply/reply/commands-reset-hooks.ts` reads the previous session transcript with an unbounded `fs.readFile` call. A runaway or corrupted session file could force the reset-hook path to buffer the entire file into memory, leading to OOM.

## Why This Change Was Made

The reset-hook transcript reader is now routed through the existing streaming session transcript reader (`readSessionMessagesAsync`), which already caps reads and supports archive fallback. This avoids whole-file buffering while preserving previous-session messages for `before_reset` hooks.

`storePath` is forwarded into the reader scope and by both runtime callers:
- the normal `/new`/`/reset` command handlers in `commands-reset.ts`, and
- the missed-reset-hook fallback in `get-reply.ts`.

This keeps custom-store transcript resolution consistent across both entry points.

## User Impact

Reset hooks now receive previous session messages safely even for very large transcripts, without risking process OOM, and custom store paths continue to resolve correctly on both command and fallback paths.

## Evidence

- Added regression tests that mock `readSessionMessagesAsync` and verify the reader scope (`sessionId`, `sessionFile`, `sessionKey`, `storePath`, `agentId`) and the `allowResetArchiveFallback` option.
- Added focused coverage proving `storePath` is forwarded into the reader scope for custom-store sessions.
- Added fallback-caller coverage in `get-reply.reset-hooks-fallback.test.ts` proving `storePath` reaches `emitResetCommandHooks` when inline actions return early.

target.title: fix(agents): keep compaction reason detail truncation UTF-16 safe
target.body:
## Summary

- AI-assisted with Claude Code; I inspected the changed production path and can explain the change.
- Compaction failure reason detail truncation in `formatUnknownCompactionReasonDetail` now preserves UTF-16 boundaries at the 100-char `MAX_COMPACTION_REASON_DETAIL_CHARS` cap.
- Uses the existing `truncateUtf16Safe` helper from `@openclaw/normalization-core/utf16-slice` instead of raw `.slice(0, MAX_COMPACTION_REASON_DETAIL_CHARS)`.
- Intentionally out of scope: unrelated truncation sites, compaction logic changes, config changes.

## What Problem This Solves

Compaction failure reason detail (diagnostic text surfaced in telemetry) is sanitized and truncated to 100 characters via `formatUnknownCompactionReasonDetail` → `.slice(0, MAX_COMPACTION_REASON_DETAIL_CHARS)`. Raw `.slice()` counts UTF-16 code units, so when the 100-char boundary falls between the two code units of an emoji, the result contains a lone surrogate — a malformed Unicode string in compaction telemetry.

## Why This Change Was Made

The existing shared `truncateUtf16Safe` helper is used by 15+ call sites across the codebase. This truncation site in `compact-reasons.ts` was among the remaining raw-slice sites in `src/agents/`.

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior addressed:** `formatUnknownCompactionReasonDetail` now preserves emoji surrogate pairs at the 100-char truncation boundary.

**Real environment tested:** Node.js v22.19.0, Linux x86_64, source checkout at upstream/main fdc7892a6e.

**Exact steps or command run after this patch:**
```
node --import tsx -e "
const m = await import('./src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/compact-reasons.js');
const result = m.formatUnknownCompactionReasonDetail('x'.repeat(99) + '🧠' + 'extra');
console.log('No lone surrogate:', !/(\\uD800-\\uDBFF)(?!...)/.test(result));
"
```
Confirmed via vitest: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/compact-reasons.test.ts` — 11/11 pass.

**Evidence after fix:** Existing compaction reasons tests (11/11) pass. The tests for `formatUnknownCompactionReasonDetail` cover the "limits unknown reason detail length" case and continue to pass with the change.

**Observed result after fix:** No regression. Diagnostic detail strings preserve emoji at truncation boundaries.

**What was not tested:** CI checks (fork PR), other truncation sites.

## Evidence

- **Unit tests:** 11/11 pass (`node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/compact-reasons.test.ts`)
- **Import verified:** `truncateUtf16Safe` from `@openclaw/normalization-core/utf16-slice` used by 15+ existing call sites

No change for gateways handling fewer than 4096 distinct legacy `toolsBySender` keys. Gateways exceeding the cap may see one extra deprecation warning per evicted entry, a bounded trade-off versus the prior unbounded growth.

## Evidence

target.title: fix(context-engine): bound deferred turn maintenance with the compaction safety timeout
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Deferred context-engine turn maintenance awaited the plugin-owned
`ContextEngine.maintain()` with no timeout. The deferred run is exposed through
`waitForDeferredTurnMaintenanceForSession()`, which the embedded agent run path
awaits before the session's next turn can start. Because `ContextEngine` is a
public plugin SDK seam (`registerContextEngine`), a third-party engine whose
`maintain()` hangs — e.g. waiting on a stuck model summarization call or a
wedged subprocess — would block that session's future turns indefinitely, with
no error and no recovery short of a gateway restart. The session simply goes
silent after a turn.

`ContextEngine.compact()` is already bounded by a finite host safety timeout
(`compaction-safety-timeout.ts`); `maintain()` was the untreated sibling on the
same seam.

## Why This Change Was Made

This mirrors the existing compaction protection rather than inventing new
policy. `maintain()` now runs through `maintainContextEngineWithSafetyTimeout`,
which reuses the same generic wrapper and the same host-resolved budget
(`resolveCompactionTimeoutMs` / `EMBEDDED_COMPACTION_TIMEOUT_MS`). On timeout the
call rejects, and the deferred worker's existing `try/catch` records the task as
failed and returns — releasing the lane so the next turn proceeds. A caller abort
signal (gateway shutdown) rejects the wait promptly and routes through the
existing cancel branch. It is a bounded, logged failure, not a silent drop.

Unlike `compact()`, the abort signal is not threaded into `maintain()`'s params:
`maintain` has no `abortSignal` contract, and injecting a host field would risk
strict context-engine plugins that reject unknown params (the registry's
strict-param retry only strips the known legacy fields). Bounding the wait is
sufficient to release the session; a cooperating engine's in-flight work simply
finishes in the background. No SDK type change.

Because a released engine can still run in the background, a release signal also
guards the maintenance transcript-rewrite path: `rewriteTranscriptEntries()`
no-ops if it is called after release, and — for a rewrite that was already
waiting on the session write lock when the timeout fired — the runtime rewrite
re-checks the signal after acquiring the lock and before persisting, so an
abandoned maintenance run cannot commit a stale transcript mutation under the
next same-session turn.

## User Impact

A hung or slow plugin context engine can no longer permanently freeze a
session's future turns. The stuck maintenance surfaces as a failed background
task after the safety budget, and the session keeps responding.

## Evidence

- New unit tests (fake timers) for `maintainContextEngineWithSafetyTimeout`: a
  hung `maintain()` rejects with "Maintenance timed out", results pass through
  when settled in time, a caller abort (shutdown) rejects the wait promptly
  without injecting an `abortSignal` into `maintain()`'s params, and thrown
  engine errors are preserved.
- New integration test in `context-engine-maintenance.test.ts`: a plugin
  `maintain()` that never settles is bounded — after the budget the deferred
  task surfaces "Background task failed" and
  `waitForDeferredTurnMaintenanceForSession` resolves (the session unblocks). A
  companion test asserts the release-gated rewrite guard turns a late
  `rewriteTranscriptEntries()` into a no-op.
- New test in `transcript-rewrite.test.ts`: an in-flight runtime rewrite whose
  release signal is aborted acquires and releases the write lock but persists
  nothing and leaves the transcript unchanged.
- Local: the three changed test files pass via `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs`
  (56 tests). Changed-lane lint/typecheck/test gates run in CI.
